planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in any reasonably drained soil; this adaptable species tolerates urban compaction, pollution, and road salt better than most shade trees.

directions: Norway Maple is a dense, round-headed shade tree with five-lobed leaves and clusters of small yellow-green flowers that open before the foliage in early spring, followed by winged samaras. It was planted extensively as a street and park tree across North America through the twentieth century because of its tolerance for poor soil, pollution, and salt, but its dense canopy and prolific self-seeding have made it invasive in many eastern forests, and several states now restrict new planting. Fall color is typically a modest yellow, less dramatic than native sugar maple. Where still permitted, it performs reliably in difficult urban sites that would stress most other large trees.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; this large European maple tolerates coastal wind and salt spray notably well, making it a traditional windbreak choice near seacoasts.

directions: Sycamore Maple is a vigorous, broad-crowned tree native to central and southern Europe, with coarse five-lobed leaves and distinctive flaking, scaly bark on older trunks that distinguishes it from other maples. Pendant chains of yellow-green flowers in spring give way to winged seed pairs held at a wide angle. It is prized in coastal and upland European landscapes for its exceptional tolerance of wind, salt spray, and poor soil, though it seeds prolifically and has naturalized in parts of the Pacific Northwest and New England. Several variegated and purple-leaved selections exist, but the straight species remains valued as a tough, fast-growing shade and shelterbelt tree.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in cool, moist, well-drained soil with some shelter from afternoon sun; the bark coloring intensifies on young wood in partial shade.

directions: Manchurian Striped Maple is a snake-bark maple from northeastern Asia grown chiefly for its smooth, blue-green bark marked with vivid vertical white striping, most striking on young trunks and branches in winter. The simple, slightly lobed leaves turn clear yellow in autumn, and small yellow flowers hang in drooping racemes in spring. It prefers a woodland-edge setting with cool roots and some protection from hot afternoon sun, where the striped bark color develops best. As a small, well-behaved understory tree it suits shade gardens and Asian-themed plantings where winter bark interest is valued alongside Acer griseum and Acer davidii.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; unlike European mountain ash, this species tolerates summer heat reasonably well.

directions: Korean Mountain Ash is unusual among Sorbus species for having simple, unlobed, birch-like leaves rather than the pinnately compound foliage typical of the genus, giving it a distinct texture in the landscape. Flat clusters of white flowers open in late spring, followed by oval red-orange berries that persist into winter and draw thrushes and waxwings. Fall color ranges from yellow to orange-red, and the smooth gray bark adds winter interest on mature trunks. It tolerates heat and heavier soils better than the European species, making it a practical mountain-ash choice for gardens outside the genus's usual cool-climate comfort zone.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to part shade in spring or fall; performs best where summers are not excessively hot and humid.

directions: Japanese Rowan carries the typical pinnate, fern-like Sorbus foliage and produces flat clusters of white spring flowers followed by heavy crops of small orange-red berries that often hang on well into winter after the leaves have dropped. Fall color is a strong orange to purplish-red, giving the species a reputation as one of the more reliable autumn-color mountain ashes for smaller gardens. It is the wild parent behind several popular selections grown for berry color and habit, but the straight species itself remains available through specialty tree nurseries and is valued for its upright, moderately narrow form in confined planting spaces.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in well-drained soil in full sun in spring or fall; benefits from shelter in exposed sites to protect the developing berry clusters from wind damage.

directions: Hubei Rowan is a graceful small tree with blue-green pinnate foliage held on slender branches, giving the crown a lighter, airier texture than most mountain ashes. White flower clusters in late spring are followed by rounded berries that open pale pink and age to white or blush-white, a color combination that makes this one of the most sought-after rowans for the white- and pink-berried border. Leaves often turn soft red to purple-red in autumn, overlapping attractively with the lingering berry display. It is a parent of several named white-berried cultivars but the species itself remains sold through specialty and mail-order tree nurseries.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container stock in well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or fall; highly cold-tolerant and well suited to prairie and northern plains plantings.

directions: Fireberry Hawthorn is a thorny, multi-stemmed North American native shrub to small tree valued for its exceptional cold hardiness, extending further north than most other hawthorn species across the Canadian prairies and northern plains. Clusters of white flowers open in late spring, followed by shiny red to orange-red fruit that ripens early and is readily eaten by grouse, waxwings, and other wildlife through fall. Its dense, thorny branching makes it useful for wildlife hedgerows and shelterbelt plantings in regions too cold for many ornamental hawthorn selections. It is sold through native plant and prairie restoration nurseries for conservation and wildlife-garden use.

planting.note: Plant container stock in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade in spring or fall; tolerates dry, chalky, and shaded sites better than most shrubby honeysuckles.

directions: European Fly Honeysuckle is a dense, twiggy, non-climbing shrub native to woodland edges across Europe and western Asia, bearing small, pale yellowish-white paired flowers in late spring that are modest compared to the genus's showier vines. The real draw is its toughness: it thrives in dry shade, chalky soil, and exposed hedgerow conditions where few other flowering shrubs persist, and it has long been used in European hedging and screening. Paired red berries follow the flowers in summer and are attractive to birds, though they are mildly toxic if eaten by people. Several compact and golden-leaved selections exist, but the straight species remains a durable, low-maintenance choice for difficult hedgerow sites.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
